title: Bull Flag
teaches: The bull flag as we trade it: a leader above the 200-day and a rising 50-day makes a fast pole, rests a few sessions in a quiet drift that holds the 20 EMA, and is bought at market when a trigger level trades, with the stop a few cents under the day's low, the first sell a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop as the planned cost.

facts.quote: A flag is a small rectangle pattern that slopes against the previous trend.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a flag is a small rectangle sloping against the prior trend.

facts.quote: Flags and pennants require evidence of a sharp advance or decline in heavy volume.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a flag needs a sharp advance on heavy volume before it.

facts.quote: The flagpole is the distance from the first resistance or support break to the high or low of the flag/pennant.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: the flagpole runs from the first break to the flag's high.

facts.quote: Ideally, these patterns will form between one and four weeks.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: ideally a flag forms in one to four weeks.

facts.quote: An expansion of volume on the resistance (support) break lends credence to the validity of the formation
facts.claim: ChartSchool: rising volume on the break adds credence.

facts.quote: Once a flag is over 12 weeks old, it would be classified as a rectangle.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a flag older than 12 weeks is a rectangle.

facts.quote: The flagpole which leads to the flag should be unusually steep and last several days.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the flagpole should be unusually steep and last several days.

facts.quote: If you don't have a straight-line (or a quick move) price run (the flagpole), then you don't have a flag.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: no straight-line run, no flag.

facts.quote: Looks like a small rectangle often tilted against the prevailing price trend.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a flag looks like a small rectangle tilted against the trend.

facts.quote: Flags are short, less than 3 weeks long. Patterns longer than that are rectangles or channels.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: flags are under 3 weeks; longer patterns are rectangles or channels.

facts.quote: Downward trend 74% (up breakouts) to 77% (down breakouts) of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: volume trends down inside a flag 74% of the time for up breakouts.

facts.quote: The best performance comes when the inbound trend is upward leading to a flag which tilts downward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the best flags tilt down after an upward trend.

facts.quote: A tight flag performs better than a loose one.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a tight flag performs better than a loose one.

facts.quote: A loose flag is one in which price meanders, pokes outside the trendline boundary, contains white space, or looks jagged.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a loose flag meanders, pokes outside its lines and looks jagged.

facts.quote: Look for a near vertical price run, preferably lasting several days.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's earnings flag: a near vertical run lasting several days.

facts.quote: Near the top of the flagpole, price consolidates and usually trends downward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's earnings flag: the pause near the top usually trends down.

facts.quote: Buy when price pierces a flag or pennant trendline (D in the figure to the right) or rises above the event pattern's high (A), but not before.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: buy the trendline pierce or the move above the pattern's high, not before.

facts.quote: A big move higher sometime in the past 1-3 months. This move can be anywhere from 30-100%+ and usually lasts a few days to a few weeks.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a big move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months comes first.

facts.quote: An orderly pullback and consolidation with higher lows and tightening range in the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: an orderly pullback with higher lows and a tightening range.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price "surfs" the rising 10- and 20-day. and sometimes toe 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: in the consolidation price surfs the rising 10- and 20-day, sometimes toes the 50-day.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day and no wider than the ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: I don't find it as effective and more skill and experience is needed.
facts.claim: Kullamagi finds anticipating the breakout less effective.

facts.quote: You should sell 1/3 to 1/2 of the position after 3-5 days, and then move the stop to break even.
facts.claim: Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days, then moves the stop to breakeven.

facts.quote: The rest of the position should be trailed with the 10- or the 20-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi trails the rest with the 10- or 20-day average.

facts.quote: they tend to move in stair steps. Meaning they will make a 20-50%+ move, pull back and go sideways for a while, then make another move.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: leaders move in stair steps: a move, a sideways rest, another move.

facts.quote: day before breakout should be narrow range day or negative day
facts.claim: Bonde: the day before the breakout should be a narrow-range or down day.

facts.quote: volume on breakout day should be higher
facts.claim: Bonde: breakout-day volume should be higher.

facts.quote: stock should close near high on breakout day
facts.claim: Bonde: the breakout day should close near its high.

facts.quote: High tight flags and bull flags are the most common continuation patterns on highly ranked stock by 65 day momentum.
facts.claim: Bonde: flags are the most common continuation patterns on momentum leaders.

facts.quote: Many of these powerful momentum movers have very shallow corrections before they continue onward.
facts.claim: Bonde: momentum movers often correct very shallowly before continuing.

facts.quote: Many times the stock will form bull flag so late in the move that you would miss bulk of the possible returns by waiting for the bull flag.
facts.claim: Bonde: a flag can form so late in a move that waiting for it misses most of the return.

facts.quote: They are typically seen right after a big, quick move.
facts.claim: Zanger: flags come right after a big, quick move.

facts.quote: Bullish flags are characterized by lower tops and lower bottoms, with the pattern slanting against the trend. But unlike wedges, their trend lines run parallel.
facts.claim: Zanger: a bull flag has lower tops and bottoms, slanting against the trend, with parallel lines.

facts.quote: Volume generally contracts during the pause with an increase on the breakout.
facts.claim: Zanger: volume contracts in the pause and rises on the breakout.

facts.quote: A minor reversal down in a bull trend. Traders expect the bull trend to resume.
facts.claim: Brooks: his bull flag is any minor reversal down in a bull trend.

facts.quote: It can be as brief as one sideways bar or it can retrace most of the most recent leg up.
facts.claim: Brooks: his bull flag can be one bar or retrace most of the last leg.

facts.quote: Most truly sound patterns consolidate a minimum of seven to eight weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: most sound bases consolidate at least seven to eight weeks; it lists no ordinary flag.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.
facts.claim: We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA: too stretched to buy.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part into a climax run on your own long.

facts.quote: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
facts.claim: D39: entry, stop and size written down before the open.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: Later sells are a judgment too: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.
facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: D38: A and B normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.

facts.claim: The close is above the 200-day on every flag session and at the entry.

facts.claim: The 50-day is above the 200-day and rising, with the close above the 50-day.

facts.claim: The first flag after a breakout or a correction is A+; the third or later without a base is B- or a pass.

facts.claim: A flag right after a parabolic burst is extended until the 10-day catches up.

facts.quote: A flag that makes a higher high than the pole is no longer a flag; it has broken out (the T3 trigger).
facts.claim: A flag that makes a higher high than the pole has broken out.

facts.quote: A flag of 16 to 20 sessions is B- at best. Past 20 sessions it is a base, judged as a flat base or a VCP.
facts.claim: A flag of 16 to 20 sessions is B- at best; past 20 it is a base.

facts.quote: The flag drifts sideways or down: the least-squares slope of the flag's highs is at or below zero. Higher highs and higher lows through the pause is a wedge up, not a flag.
facts.claim: The flag drifts sideways or down; higher highs and higher lows is a wedge up, not a flag.

facts.quote: The flag's average daily range (high minus low, as a percent of the close) is smaller than the pole's.
facts.claim: The flag's average daily range is smaller than the pole's.

facts.quote: No flag session closes red with volume of 1.5 times its 50-day average or more. One such day drops the grade; two end the flag.
facts.claim: One heavy red day in the flag drops the grade; two end the flag.

facts.claim: Every flag close holds the rising 21-day EMA; an intraday undercut that closes back above is allowed.

facts.claim: Riding the 9 or 10-day through the flag is A+; tagging the 20 or 21-day and reclaiming is A or B.

facts.quote: An inside day or a narrow-range day right before the trigger is the A+ tightness cue: it gives a nearer stop.
facts.claim: An inside day or narrow-range day right before the trigger is the A+ tightness cue.

facts.quote: A market order when the trigger level trades, regular hours only. Set the alert at the level the night before.

facts.claim: The flag's low is the invalidation, not the default stop.

facts.quote: Before entry: two or more heavy red days in the flag, each on 1.5 times average volume or more. Distribution, not a rest.

facts.claim: The third flag in a short run without a base: wait for the base.

facts.quote: After the entry, a close under the flag's low means the idea is dead; the stop has normally been hit well before it.
facts.claim: After entry a close under the flag's low means the idea is dead; the stop is hit well before.

walkthroughs.title: SHOP, May 2020: eight quiet days after a double
steps: SHOP doubled off the 2020 low in 12 days, to 66.57. Then it rested eight sessions between 59.50 and 66.26.
Every close held its rising short-term averages, on lighter volume than the pole. It's over the 50 and 200-day too.
May 4 it trades over the prior day's high. Buy at market, 62.80, still under the flag's high. Stop 61.65, 1.8% away.
Lose the day's low and we're out. Instead it ran 41.7R. A runner like that, you trail on the 9 EMA.

walkthroughs.title: AMD, August 2018: four quiet days after an earnings gap
steps: AMD gapped up on earnings and ran 29% in 14 days to 20.28. Then it rested four days on light volume.
Short and shallow, 18.73 to 20.10, only 7.6% deep. A fast pole on a catalyst is the kind I want.
August 21 the prior day's high breaks. We buy at market, 20.09. Stop just under the day's low, 19.81, 1.4% away.
Sell some into a push, day 3 or later, and trail the rest. AMD went 20 to 34 in five weeks.

walkthroughs.title: RARE, May 2015: a staircase, one step at a time
steps: RARE ran 53% in 13 days to 85.93. Then it rests four days, 80.25 to 85.79, right on its short-term average.
May 27 it takes out the prior day's high before the flag's high even breaks. We buy right there at market, 83.26.
Stop a few cents under the low, 81.18, 2.5% away. Full size at one price, one stop. No starter piece.
Then a second leg as big as the first, 25.9R at its best. Sell into strength and trail what's left.

questions.q: What did the stock do right before this rest?
choices: A sharp, fast run up
A slow, steady grind up
A long, flat base of weeks
A quick drop on bad news
questions.answer: A sharp, fast run up
questions.why: A sharp, fast run up. That's the pole. RARE ran 53% in 13 days to 85.93, then sat four days between 80.25 and 85.79. A flag only means something when there's a hurried run to rest from. The run shows real demand, and the short rest gives you a tight spot to risk against. A slow grind into a pause is just a pullback.
questions.lesson_line: No pole, no flag. Find the run first, then look at the rest.

wrong.A quick drop on bad news: A drop isn't a pole. A bull flag rests after a run up.
wrong.A slow, steady grind up: A steady grind has no pole. The pause after it is just a pullback to the averages, a different setup.
wrong.A long, flat base of weeks: A base can come before the run. The flag is the short rest after the run.

questions.simple: A flag rests after a sharp, fast run. With no run before it, a pause is just a pause.

deeper.trap: A neat, tight pause isn't enough on its own. Bulkowski is blunt: if you don't have a straight-line run, you don't have a flag. ChartSchool also wants a sharp advance on heavy volume before it.

reasons: +1 fixed before (the Bulkowski steep-pole quote was added to the cited facts)

questions.story: The day before the buy. This leader has rested four sessions near its highs. Look at what the chart did right before that rest.

questions.q: Which way is this rest drifting?
choices: Sideways to down, against the run
Up, with higher highs and lows
Straight down toward the 200-day
Dead flat, a tilt down fails it
questions.answer: Sideways to down, against the run
questions.why: Sideways to down, leaning against the run. That's what a flag does. AMD topped at 20.28, then held 18.73 to 20.10 for four days. The highs stopped climbing and nobody dumped it either. That lean back lets the 9 EMA catch up, so you're not buying something stretched. If the highs and lows keep rising through the pause, it never rested. That's a wedge up, and I pass.
questions.lesson_line: The flag leans back against the run. Up and to the right is something else.

wrong.Up, with higher highs and lows: Rising highs and lows through the pause is a wedge up. It never rested, so it's not a flag.
wrong.Straight down toward the 200-day: A slide that deep isn't a rest. It gives back the run the flag is supposed to rest from.
wrong.Dead flat, a tilt down fails it: A small tilt down is normal, even a plus. The pause just can't climb.

questions.simple: A flag leans sideways or down against the run. A pause that keeps climbing is a wedge up, not a rest.

reasons: three agreeing web sources, a stable definition

questions.story: The day before the buy. This leader ran up hard, then rested four sessions. Look at where the highs and lows of that rest go.

deeper.counter: ChartSchool calls a flag a small rectangle that slopes against the previous trend. Zanger describes lower tops and lower bottoms with parallel lines. Bulkowski finds the best flags tilt down after an upward trend.

questions.q: You buy a flag break at 62.80. Your stop goes a few cents under that day's low.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The low of the day, LOD, is where today's buy has clearly failed. That's the nearest honest line on the chart. Put the stop a few cents under it, not right on it, so a tick to the low doesn't shake you out. SHOP in 2020 filled at 62.80 with the stop at 61.65, only 1.8% away. If your plan was the prior day's low, same idea. Stop first, then the size comes from it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first. A few cents under the low of the day.
questions.simple: True. The low of the day is where the buy has clearly failed, so the stop sits a few cents under it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A flag is ours only above the ___-day simple moving average, the line below which we buy no longs.
questions.why: 200. We buy no stock below its 200-day simple moving average. The close holds above it on every flag session and at the entry.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, every day of the flag. Below it there is no flag to buy.
questions.simple: The line is the 200-day. We buy no longs below it, and a flag only counts above it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: What is volume doing while this flag rests?
choices: It dries up, far below the run
It stays as heavy as the run
It builds as buyers pile in
It spikes on the red days
questions.answer: It dries up, far below the run
questions.why: It dries up. BB ran 37% in 4 days to 84.10, then rested on 0.28x the run's volume. That's the picture I want. The holders who wanted out are mostly gone, and nobody's dumping it. So when buyers come back through the trigger, there's not much supply in the way. It raises the grade. It's not a must, though. A tight flag without it still gets bought.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet in the flag, loud on the break. Volume that dries up raises the grade.

wrong.It stays as heavy as the run: A rest as loud as the run isn't a quiet rest. Look again, volume dried up to a fraction of the run's.
wrong.It builds as buyers pile in: Volume picks up on the break, not in the rest. Here it dried up.
wrong.It spikes on the red days: No heavy red days here. Those would be a warning, a sign big holders are selling.

questions.simple: Volume dries up while the flag rests. Few holders are selling, so I like it, and it raises the grade.

deeper.example: Bulkowski finds volume trending down in 74% of flags that break out upward, so it's the normal picture, not a law. Zanger saw the same thing: quiet in the pause, more on the breakout. PANW rested four days on half the pole's volume.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-006, how strict the volume rule is)
+2 a statistic that changes (Bulkowski's 74%, updated 2020)

questions.story: The day before the buy. This leader ran up on heavy volume, then rested four sessions. Look at the volume bars under that rest.

questions.q: Your alert at yesterday's high goes off at 10:05. You buy it at market right there.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The level trading is the buy, so you want in right when it trades. Park a limit order under the level and the stock can leave without you. Then you're tempted to chase it. Set the alert the night before so you're ready, and only buy in regular hours. One more check before you click: we never pay more than 4% over the buy point.
questions.lesson_line: Alert tonight, market order when it trades, regular hours only.
questions.simple: True. The level trading is the signal, and a market order gets you in while a limit can miss it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)

questions.q: A leader broke out of a base, then flagged. It has flagged twice more since, with no real base in between. Which flag was the best buy?
choices: The first, right after the breakout
The third, once the trend is proven
Any of them, the shape is the same
The deepest one, it's the cheapest
questions.answer: The first, right after the breakout
questions.why: The first one. It comes right after the base breakout, or right after a market correction, early in the run. Most of the move is still ahead of you. By the third flag the stock has run a long way with no real rest, and less is left to give. I'd rather be involved early. On a third flag with no proper base, I wait for the base.
questions.lesson_line: First flag, best flag. Each one after it comes later in the run.

wrong.The third, once the trend is proven: A proven trend is a late one. By the third flag the run is old, so I wait for a proper base.
wrong.Any of them, the shape is the same: The shape repeats. Where it sits in the run doesn't, and early is where the move is.
wrong.The deepest one, it's the cheapest: Deeper isn't better. It gives back more of the run, and cheap isn't a reason to buy.

questions.simple: The first flag after a breakout comes early in the run, so most of the move is still ahead.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed grade row, not a web source
+1 fixed before (a choice was shortened)

deeper.counter: Bonde warns a flag can form so late in a move that waiting for it misses the bulk of the return. Kullamagi notes leaders move in stair steps: a move, a sideways rest, then another move.

questions.q: Two flags look the same. One stock has an RS rating of 92 and sits in a strong group. The other is rated 40. Which do you buy?
choices: The 92, in the strong group
The 40, it has room to catch up
Either one, the shape is what pays
Whichever is louder in the news
questions.answer: The 92, in the strong group
questions.why: The 92. RS rating ranks a stock's strength against the whole market, so the 92 is a leader and the 40 is a laggard. A flag is a rest inside a run that's already strong. In a leader, the pause is strength resting. In a laggard it's weakness resting. We buy leaders, rated 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. Our RS screens in the Screener pull these names up for you.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the leader's flag. A laggard's flag is just a laggard resting.

wrong.Either one, the shape is what pays: The shape alone doesn't pay. The edge comes from the leader, the catalyst, the market and how you manage it.
wrong.The 40, it has room to catch up: Catching up isn't a setup. A flag continues what a stock was already doing, and this one was lagging.
wrong.Whichever is louder in the news: Loud isn't leading. We rank by RS and by group strength, not by headlines.

questions.simple: The leader. A flag rests a run that's already strong, and the high RS stock is where that strength is.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

deeper.counter: Bonde finds high tight flags and bull flags are the most common continuation patterns on stocks ranked high for momentum.

questions.q: You buy a flag break at 62.80. The flag's low is 59.50. That flag low makes a good, tight stop.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. From 62.80 down to 59.50 is more than 5%, past what we'll accept on a stop. We like 1% to 3%. On this exact trade SHOP's stop went a few cents under the low of the day, at 61.65, just 1.8% away. Same buy, a much tighter stop, so more shares for the same risk. The flag's low still matters. It's where the whole idea is wrong, not where your trade is.
questions.lesson_line: The flag low is where the idea dies. The low of the day is where the trade does.
questions.simple: False. The flag low sits far under the buy, and the low of the day gives a much nearer stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62) and the card's proposed stop line (D-002)

questions.q: Day three of a flag. The stock trades up through the pole's high, the top of the whole run. What are you looking at now?
choices: A breakout, not a flag anymore
Still a flag, the rest goes on
A failed flag, so it's dead
A wedge up, so you pass
questions.answer: A breakout, not a flag anymore
questions.why: A breakout. The pole's high is the lid on the whole move. Trade through it and buyers have beaten the old top, so the rest is over. Now you judge it as a breakout. Same discipline as always: buy at market as it goes through, and never pay more than 4% over the level. Missed it by more than that, let it go.
questions.lesson_line: The pole top is the lid. Through it, the rest is over.

wrong.Still a flag, the rest goes on: A flag that makes a higher high than the pole has broken out. The rest ended the moment it went through.
wrong.A failed flag, so it's dead: Clearing the pole's top is the opposite of failing. A close under the flag's low is what kills it.
wrong.A wedge up, so you pass: A wedge climbs through the whole pause. One push through the pole's high is a breakout.

questions.simple: Trading over the pole's high means buyers beat the old top. The rest is over, so it's a breakout now.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (the card's line, c05)

questions.q: Two tight flags look the same. One sits on a rising 50-day. The other's 50-day is rolling over. They're equally good buys.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. I want the 50-day pointing up. A rising 50 says the trend under the flag is still up, and a flag is just a pause inside that trend. When the 50 rolls over, the trend is fading, and the same pause has less behind it. I'd take the one on the rising 50. It's a plus I look for, and the price still has to sit above the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Check the 50-day before you trust the flag. You want it pointing up.
questions.simple: False. A rising 50-day means the trend under the flag is still up, and a rolling one has less behind it.

reasons: one cited fact only (c02)
a card proposal, not a rulebook rule (B26 is only the 200-day line)

deeper.counter: Bulkowski finds the best flags come when the trend into the flag is upward and the flag itself tilts down.

questions.q: That last bar is an inside day. What does it give you for tomorrow's buy?
choices: A nearer stop for the buy
A warning the flag is failing
A reason to buy it right now
A wider stop to ride the noise
questions.answer: A nearer stop for the buy
questions.why: A nearer stop. An inside day trades inside the prior day's range, so the stock is getting tight right at the trigger. When it goes through, the low of the day sits close under your buy. TSEM did exactly this: bought at 66.62, stop 64.78. A nearer stop lets the same risk buy more shares. I love seeing a quiet, tight day right before the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A tight day before the trigger is a small stop waiting to be used.

wrong.A warning the flag is failing: A quiet, narrow day is what a healthy rest looks like. Heavy red days are the warning.
wrong.A reason to buy it right now: The inside day sets it up. The buy still waits for the trigger level to trade.
wrong.A wider stop to ride the noise: It's the other way around. Small bars put the low of the day close, so the stop is nearer.

questions.simple: A tight day right before the trigger puts the stop close, so the same risk buys more shares.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's tightness cue, with Bonde as the only web source

questions.story: The day before the buy. A leader has rested a few sessions after its run. Check the last bar: its high is under the prior day's high, and its low is above the prior day's low.

deeper.counter: Bonde wants the day before a breakout to be a narrow-range day or a down day.

questions.q: You buy a flag break at 48.98, your full size, with one stop. If it dips under your buy, you don't add.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. One price, one stop, one size. You know your loss before you ever click buy. Add on a dip and that number changes after the stock has already gone against you. That's how a small planned loss turns into a big one. We buy the full position at one spot. No starter, and you never add to a loser.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, one size. No starter, no adding to a loser.
questions.simple: True. Buying it all at one price with one stop keeps the loss you planned, and adding on a dip grows it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)
+1 fixed before (the lesson line read as permission to add)

questions.q: When do you make your first sell?
choices: Into a push of 3, 5 or 7 days
At 3R, every time, no matter what
Only at the measured move target
Never, let the whole thing ride
questions.answer: Into a push of 3, 5 or 7 days
questions.why: Into the push, by judgment. Your risk is the gap from 66.62 down to 64.78. I very rarely sell on day 1. I wait until day 3 at the earliest, and I like selling some into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. That push can be 10, 12, even 20R. Selling part into strength banks a real gain while the rest keeps working. TSEM took nine sessions to reach 3R, then ran past 100.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment. Sell into a strong push of a few days.

wrong.Only at the measured move target: A measured move is a guess at a number. I sell into the push the stock actually gives me.
wrong.At 3R, every time, no matter what: There's no fixed 3R sell. Sometimes it's R based, sometimes it's day based. It's a judgment.
wrong.Never, let the whole thing ride: We sell part into strength and trail what's left. Holding it all gives back too much when it turns.

questions.simple: Sell some into a strong push of a few days, so you bank real gain while the rest keeps running.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days, then moves his stop to breakeven. Close to what we do: take some early and trail the rest.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.story: You bought the flag break at 66.62 with the stop at 64.78. Over the next few days it starts to push higher.

questions.q: The closes ride the 9 EMA and never tag the 20 EMA. How do you read this rest?
choices: Strong, buyers never let it sag
Weak, it never tested support
Same as a dip to the 20 EMA
Not a flag, it has to tag the 20
questions.answer: Strong, buyers never let it sag
questions.why: Strong. Every little dip gets bought right at the 9 EMA. Buyers won't even let it sag to the 20. That's more demand than a rest that drops to the 20 EMA and bounces. Both can be good flags. I just rate the one riding the 9 higher. UIS drifted seven days like this on half the run's volume, then cleared the flag high on 2.3x volume.
questions.lesson_line: Riding the 9 EMA reads stronger than tagging the 20 and bouncing.

wrong.Weak, it never tested support: Not testing the 20 EMA isn't a flaw. Buyers simply never let it get there.
wrong.Same as a dip to the 20 EMA: Both can be bought, but riding the 9 shows more demand. I grade it higher.
wrong.Not a flag, it has to tag the 20: Tagging the 20 EMA is allowed, never required. The tighter it rides, the better.

questions.simple: Riding the 9 EMA is the stronger look, because buyers step in at every small dip.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed grade row
+1 fixed before (the old B- note leaned on a pending rule)

questions.story: The day before the buy. A leader rests for several sessions after a run. Watch where the closes sit against the 9 EMA and the 20 EMA.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi describes price surfing the rising 10- and 20-day through the consolidation, sometimes toeing the 50-day.

questions.q: How would you describe this four-day rest?
choices: Tight, small bars, no wild swings
Loose, the bars wander and poke out
Too short, four days isn't a flag
Tight, only because the pole was big
questions.answer: Tight, small bars, no wild swings
questions.why: Tight. Four small bars inside a 2.9% range, on about half the pole's volume. That's as clean as a flag gets. Tight matters for two reasons. It shows nobody's in a hurry to sell. And it puts the low of the day close to your buy. PANW filled at 48.98 with the stop at 48.29, a 1.4% stop, and later reached 26.4R.
questions.lesson_line: Tight means smaller bars than the run. Jagged means pass.

wrong.Tight, only because the pole was big: A big pole doesn't make a rest tight. Tight comes from the rest's own small bars.
wrong.Loose, the bars wander and poke out: Loose looks jagged and wanders outside its lines. These bars stayed in a narrow 2.9% band.
wrong.Too short, four days isn't a flag: Four sessions is a normal flag. AMD, RARE, BB and PANW all rested four days.

questions.story: The day before the buy. After a 36% pole, this stock paused four sessions in a 2.9% range. Look at the size of the bars in the rest.
questions.simple: Tight. Small bars mean no one's rushing to sell, and they let the stop sit close to the buy.

deeper.example: Bulkowski finds a tight flag performs better than a loose one. He describes a loose one as meandering, poking outside its trendlines and looking jagged.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's range rule
+1 fixed before (a wrong count of four-day rests was corrected)

questions.q: Day four of a flag. At noon it dips under the 20 EMA, then closes back above it on quiet volume. Is the flag still good?
choices: Yes, the close held the line
No, the flag is over, step aside
Weaker, it's a heavy red day
Yes, the 20 EMA doesn't matter
questions.answer: Yes, the close held the line
questions.why: Yes. The close is what counts, and it closed back above the line. Buyers stepped in and defended the 20 EMA the same day. An intraday undercut that closes back above is fine, and it's often the buy. What I'd worry about is a close under the line that doesn't get reclaimed. Quiet volume on the dip is a good sign too. Nobody was dumping it.
questions.lesson_line: An undercut that closes back above the line is fine. The close is what counts.

wrong.No, the flag is over, step aside: The close is the verdict, and it closed back above the line. Nothing broke.
wrong.Weaker, it's a heavy red day: A heavy red day closes red on big volume. This one closed back above the line on quiet volume.

Buy, the trend is proven
Buy, with a tighter stop
Wait for a fourth flag

Up to 12 weeks, then a rectangle
Under 1 week, else a rectangle
At least 7 to 8 weeks, like a base

ChartSchool ideally sees one to four weeks and calls a flag over 12 weeks old a rectangle. IBD says most sound bases take at least seven to eight weeks. A rest that long is a base, not a flag.

Third flag A+; the trend is proven

questions.q: Which breakout do you trust more?

VQRT, 0.7x volume, closes mid-range
Same, only the level matters
Neither, a break needs news

Both triggered, and you'd own both at the level. But LZNB's break raises the grade. Volume is a plus, not a must. Your stop still sits under the low of the day either way.
questions.lesson_line: Big volume and a close at the high make a break more trusted. Quiet and mid-range, less.

wrong.Same, only the level matters: The level is the trigger. How the day trades after it, volume and close, tells you how strong the break is.

Pull the stop in so the size fits
Full size, risk a bit more
Buy a starter, add the rest later

The size comes from the stop, never the other way around. Pull the stop up just to fit more shares and normal noise takes you out of a good trade. Past 5%, I'd mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

Yes, 12% above is normal
No, five days is too short

Orange is only A+ setups, our cleanest. Red is mostly cash. In a weaker market more breakouts fail, because the market isn't backing them. So I still take the best of these flags, just with less money on each and fewer at once.
questions.lesson_line: Yellow means the same flags with less money behind them.

wrong.Only the grade changes, not size: The grade is how clean the setup is. The market reading changes your size and how many you hold.
wrong.No flags at all until Green: That's closer to Red, which is mostly cash. Yellow still trades, smaller and fewer.
wrong.Nothing, they're first flags: Full risk belongs to Green. A great setup in a Yellow market still gets less money.

questions.story: The market reading is the app's market filter: Green, Yellow, Orange or Red. It just turned Yellow. Three clean first flags on your list hit their triggers.
questions.simple: Smaller and fewer. A weaker market backs fewer breakouts, so you risk less on each one.

questions.q: What takes out the rest of this fast mover?
choices: A close under the 9 EMA
A dip under the flag low
A close under the 50-day
Any red day, even a small one
questions.answer: A close under the 9 EMA
questions.why: A close under the 9 EMA. A fast mover like this rides that line the whole way up. As long as it closes above it, the push is alive. A close below says it's stalled, so you sell what's left. Not on an intraday dip, on the close. For a steadier mover we give it room to the 20 EMA instead. RARE rested right on its fast average, then ran a second leg the same size as the first.
questions.lesson_line: What's left rides the line. The close below it is the exit, not a dip under it.

wrong.A dip under the flag low: Price hits your trail long before the flag low. What's left sells on a close under the 9 EMA.
wrong.A close under the 50-day: The 50-day is way too loose for a fast mover. Our trail is the 9 EMA, or the 20 for steadier names.
wrong.Any red day, even a small one: One red day is noise. The close under the trail line is the signal.

questions.simple: A close under the 9 EMA, because a fast mover rides that line, and a close below says the push stalled.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook trail default (E52), which is adjustable

questions.story: You bought the flag break at 83.26 with the stop at 81.18. You've sold some into a push. The rest is still riding a fast move.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi trails the rest with the 10- or 20-day moving average. Our lines are the 9 and 20 EMA.

questions.q: How do you grade that stop?
choices: It did its job, a small loss
It proved the entry was wrong
Wrong, it should wait for a close
Too tight, widen it next time
questions.answer: It did its job, a small loss
questions.why: It did its job. You lost what you planned and kept your money for the next trigger. STZ ran to 50 without us, and that stings. That's hindsight. Stops get hit a lot on flags. Our own research found seven in ten fixed-stop entries come back to the stop before 3R. A small stop keeps each one cheap. The answer is the next trigger, not a wider stop.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working. The answer is the next trigger.

wrong.It proved the entry was wrong: One stop-out proves nothing. Seven in ten fixed-stop entries come back to the stop before 3R. That's the cost of the plan.
wrong.Wrong, it should wait for a close: The stop is a real order with the broker. It sells when it trades, no waiting for a close.
wrong.Too tight, widen it next time: It sat a few cents under the low of the day, right where it belongs. A wider stop just makes every loss bigger.

questions.story: You bought the flag break at 44.34 with the stop at 43.55. It reaches 0.85R, then day two's low of 43.07 takes your stop. The stock later runs to 50.
questions.simple: The stop did its job. Stops get hit a lot, so a small planned loss keeps each one cheap.

deeper.trap: The later run to 50 tempts you to call the stop wrong. That's hindsight. A stop is judged by the plan, not by what came after. The same small stop on the next trigger is still the rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)
the seven-in-ten count is our own scan

questions.q: How many R are you up? One R is your fill minus your stop.
questions.answer: 5R
questions.why: 5R. One R is your risk per share, 48.98 minus 48.29. Your gain is 52.43 minus 48.98, which is 3.45. Divide that 3.45 by one R and you're up 5R. Think in R, not dollars. It tells you what the move is worth against what you risked. Our rules are written in R too. Breakeven moves come between 2R and 5R, and up 5R is what it takes to hold through a report.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. Breakeven and the earnings hold are both written in R.
questions.simple: You're up 5R. The gain is five times the risk per share, and our rules are written in R.

reasons: a computed key

choices: 6R
5R
7R

wrong.3.45R: That's the dollar gain per share. Divide it by your risk per share to get R.
wrong.7R: That's the percent gain. R compares the gain to your risk, not to the price.

questions.q: What's your stop now?
choices: First 30-min low, out past 2R
Sell it all at the open
Move it up to 62.80, the entry
Buy more to lower your cost
questions.answer: First 30-min low, out past 2R
questions.why: The low of the first 30 minutes is your new stop. Opening prints on a gap day swing wildly, and selling blind at the open can mean selling the low. So you let the first 30-minute bar trade, and its low becomes the stop. One ceiling: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you're out. It's the one time the stop can move down. Everywhere else it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets 30 minutes, not a new opinion.

wrong.Sell it all at the open: The open on a gap day is the wildest print of the day. The gap rule waits for the first 30 minutes.
wrong.Move it up to 62.80, the entry: Breakeven is for a winner, anywhere from 2R to 5R or at the first sell. This one is under your fill, so a stop at 62.80 sits above the price.
wrong.Buy more to lower your cost: That's averaging down, adding to a loser. A gap against you is never a reason to buy more.

questions.story: Your flag long filled at 62.80 with the stop at 61.65. Next morning it opens at 61.10 on sector news, right through your stop.
questions.simple: The open after a gap swings wildly, so the first 30-minute low is your stop. Past 2R, you're out.

deeper.trap: The pull is to dump it at once or to hope. The rule does neither. It waits for the first 30-minute bar and uses its low as the stop. If that low puts the loss past 2R, you're out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook gap rule (B20)
fixed before: the open was moved so the 2R ceiling does not apply

questions.q: By our card's pole test, bull flag or high tight flag?
choices: A high tight flag
An ordinary bull flag
A long flat base
A simple pullback
questions.answer: A high tight flag
questions.why: A high tight flag. Measure the pole first: a high tight flag follows a near-double, and a bull flag follows a smaller run. A run of 110% is more than a double. A 15-session rest is also too short for a flat base, which rests at least 25. Bonde names both flags as the momentum leader's patterns.
questions.lesson_line: The pole names the setup. A near-double is the other lesson.

wrong.An ordinary bull flag: A 110% run in six weeks is more than a double. That pole belongs to the high tight flag.
wrong.A long flat base: Fifteen sessions is too short for a flat base, which rests at least 25.
wrong.A simple pullback: A pullback has no pole. This stock ran 110% first, so there is a pole to name.

questions.story: The stock ran 110% in six weeks on a product launch. Now it pauses 15 sessions a little under the high.
questions.simple: The pole decides it. A run of 110% is more than a double, so this is a high tight flag.

deeper.trap: A big run is not enough on its own. Measure the pole, then count the rest. Here the run is 110% in six weeks and the rest is 15 sessions. A near-double with a short rest is the high tight flag. A smaller run is the bull flag.

reasons: a number rule that is still pending (D-048, D-049)

questions.q: A rest this long. Is it still a bull flag?
choices: No, a rest this long is a base
Yes, the price is still holding up
No, it's a wedge up, highs rising
No, it's a failed flag, it's dead
questions.answer: No, a rest this long is a base
questions.why: No, it's a base now. A flag is a short rest after a fast run, a few sessions, maybe a couple of weeks. Nine weeks isn't a pause anymore. It has built its own pattern, so judge it like a base, with its own top to buy through. Don't sit in a forever flag waiting for it to act like one.
questions.lesson_line: A rest measured in weeks is a base. Count the sessions before you name it.

wrong.Yes, the price is still holding up: Holding up is good, but nine weeks is far past a flag. It's built a base.
wrong.No, it's a wedge up, highs rising: A wedge up climbs through the pause. This rest has hardly moved.
wrong.No, it's a failed flag, it's dead: Nothing broke. It just rested too long to be a flag.

questions.story: After a 35% run the stock has rested nine weeks and still hasn't triggered. Price has hardly moved.
questions.simple: It's a base now. A flag is a short rest after a fast run, and nine weeks is far too long.

deeper.counter: Sources differ on where a flag ends. ChartSchool ideally sees one to four weeks. Bulkowski says under 3 weeks, and calls longer patterns rectangles or channels. Nine weeks is past both.

reasons: the flag length is still pending (D-045)
rests on a held decision
the flat ceiling tell is the card's alone

questions.q: Which pattern is this?
choices: A VCP setup
A bull flag
A high tight flag
A flat base
questions.answer: A VCP setup
questions.why: A VCP, a volatility contraction pattern. Look for shrinking pullbacks. A flag is one short drift on lighter volume. A VCP strings several pullbacks, each smaller than the last, before its pivot. Here three pullbacks over 30 sessions each shrink.
questions.lesson_line: One drift is a flag. A string of shrinking swings is the VCP lesson.

wrong.A bull flag: Three pullbacks over 30 sessions is not one short drift. That is the volatility contraction pattern.
wrong.A high tight flag: The story gives no doubling pole, and the rest is too long and too structured for a flag.
wrong.A flat base: A flat base is a long, flat box with a tapped ceiling. These pullbacks shrink each time, which is the VCP tell.

questions.story: Over 30 sessions the stock makes three pullbacks, each shallower than the last, volume drying on each. The last one is a few percent deep.
questions.simple: Three pullbacks that each get smaller make a VCP. A flag is only one short drift.

deeper.trap: The lookalike to rule out is the flat base, which is a long, flat box with a tapped ceiling. A VCP is different: each pullback is smaller than the one before it, and the pivot sits at the end. Count the pullbacks before you name it.

reasons: the VCP tell rests on the card's line alone
fixed before: choices rebalanced

questions.q: What setup is this pause?
choices: A moving-average pullback
A bull flag after a steep run
A flat base resting for weeks
A wedge up along the 20 EMA
questions.answer: A moving-average pullback
questions.why: A moving-average pullback. There's no pole here. META rose 18.2% over 20 sessions, a steady climb with no burst. Then it paused neatly by the 20 EMA. Nice-looking pause, but with no fast run before it, it's not a flag. It's a pullback to the average in an uptrend, and that setup has its own rules. Name it right and you trade it right.
questions.lesson_line: No run, no flag. A tidy pause with no pole is a pullback.

wrong.A flat base resting for weeks: A flat base rests many weeks. This pause lasted five sessions.
wrong.A bull flag after a steep run: The climb was steady, not steep. No pole, no flag.
wrong.A wedge up along the 20 EMA: A wedge makes higher highs and lows through the pause. This one stayed flat above the 20 EMA.

questions.story: The day before a possible buy. This leader climbed steadily for about a month, with no burst. Then it rested five sessions, flat, just above its 20 EMA.
questions.simple: With only a steady climb before it, there's no pole, so the pause is a pullback, not a flag.

deeper.trap: Bulkowski: if you don't have a straight-line run, you don't have a flag. A leader that climbs steadily and then pauses neatly has nothing sharp to rest from.

reasons: the pole size is still pending (D-029), but the key holds under every option
fixed before: a flagged question

questions.q: What is this rest now that it has run about a month?
choices: A base, no longer a flag
A bull flag, still intact
A flag that failed
A bull flag, just a slow one
questions.answer: A base, no longer a flag
questions.why: A base. A flag is a short rest from a fast run. Bulkowski says flags are short and that longer patterns are rectangles or channels. After about a month of drifting, the rest is its own pattern, judged by the base rules. It stayed shallow on quiet volume, so nothing failed. It simply stopped being a flag.
questions.lesson_line: A flag is a short rest. A rest that runs on for weeks is a base.

wrong.A flag that failed: Nothing failed. It held shallow on quiet volume. It just stopped being a flag and became a base.
wrong.A bull flag, still intact: A flag is a short rest. A month of drifting has outgrown it, however neat it looks.
wrong.A bull flag, just a slow one: There is no slow flag. A rest this long is judged as a base.

questions.story: A leader made a 30% run, then rested only 6.6% deep on quiet volume. The rest is now about a month old and has not triggered.
questions.simple: A rest this long is a base, not a flag, because a flag is a short rest from a fast run.

deeper.trap: A rest that runs on is judged as a base, not a flag. It can still be a good setup, only under different rules. Do not let a clean, quiet look keep the word flag alive.

reasons: rests on the card's 20-session line (c06)
21 sessions is a base under D-045 options A and B; option C (up to 2 months) would make it a flag

questions.q: A flag that closed under its 21-day EMA on two straight sessions can still be bought on the next prior-day-high break.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Two closes under the 21-day EMA end the flag. The buy needs a flag that is still on; the next one is a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the line twice and the flag is gone. Wait for the next setup, not the next tick.

questions.q: What did the stop do?
choices: Its job; the leader simply failed
Cost you; it needed more room
Nothing; you should have added lower
questions.answer: Its job; the leader simply failed
questions.why: Its job. The trigger day closed at the low of its range, the next session's low took the stop, and the loss was 1.78%. A planned loss is the system working.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped out for 1.78%. That is the cost of being there for the ones that run.

wrong.Cost you; it needed more room: More room is a bigger loss on the same failed break. The stop only moves up.
wrong.Nothing; you should have added lower: No adding, no averaging down. A failed break is an exit, not a sale.

questions.story: You buy the prior-day-high break at 276.33, stop 271.41. The day closes at the low of its range, 271.99. Next morning the low of 270.60 takes you out.

questions.q: Bought at 66.62, stop 64.78. You sell a third at 72.14. How many R did that third bank?
questions.why: 3R. The gain divided by the fill minus the stop. TSEM took nine sessions to get there and then ran past 100.
questions.lesson_line: Count every exit in R. The first third is 3R.

questions.q: It's day 4 and still pushing. How do you pick your first sell?
choices: Judgment, sell some into the push
Hold every share to the trail
Sell the whole thing at 3R
A fixed third at 3R, every time
questions.answer: Judgment, sell some into the push
questions.why: By judgment, selling some into the push. Day 4 of a strong push is right in the window I like. I very rarely sell on day 1. I wait until day 3 at the earliest. A 3, 5 or 7 day push is often the best spot, and so is about 5 to 10R. Selling part into strength banks a real gain while the rest rides the trail.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into strength. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed level.

wrong.Hold every share to the trail: Holding it all gives back a lot when it turns. We sell part into strength and trail the rest.
wrong.Sell the whole thing at 3R: Selling it all throws away the trail. The first sell is part of the position, into strength.
wrong.A fixed third at 3R, every time: There's no fixed third at 3R. Sometimes it's R based, sometimes it's day based. It's a judgment.

questions.story: A four-day flag after a near-vertical pole. You bought at 80.41 with the stop at 78.66. The stock keeps pushing higher, day after day.
questions.simple: Sell some into the push by judgment. It banks real gain while the rest rides the trail.

deeper.example: BB ran 37% in 4 days into this flag and rested on 0.28x the pole's volume. When a stock like that pushes for days, you sell some into it and trail the rest.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook trims (B19, E51)
the 5R level is adjustable

questions.q: Do you hold it through the report?
choices: No, I hold only if up 5R
Yes, it was an A+ setup
Yes, with the stop at breakeven
No, I hold only if up 3R
questions.answer: No, I hold only if up 5R
questions.why: No. A report can gap a stock right past any stop, even a breakeven one. So we only hold through earnings when the trade is up 5R. That cushion is big enough that a bad gap still doesn't turn a winner into a loss. You're up 2R, nowhere near it. Take it off before the report. If it sets up again after, buy it on a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Five R buys the ticket through earnings. Two R doesn't.

wrong.Yes, it was an A+ setup: The grade doesn't stop a gap. The line is 5R, and you're up 2R.
wrong.Yes, with the stop at breakeven: A gap can jump a breakeven stop overnight. The line is 5R.
wrong.No, I hold only if up 3R: 3R isn't the line. We hold through a report only when up 5R.

questions.story: Your flag long is up 2R, and the company reports tomorrow after the close. You graded the setup A+, our cleanest kind.
questions.simple: No. A report can gap past any stop, so we only hold through one with a 5R cushion.

deeper.trap: A breakeven stop feels like free protection, but an overnight gap can open below it. Then the gap rule makes the first 30-minute low your stop, and a loss past 2R in that time means you're out.

reasons: the key rests on one fact (h08)
rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Al Brooks calls any small pullback in a bull trend a bull flag. So his bull flag and ours are the same setup.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Same name, different idea. Brooks uses bull flag for any minor pullback in a bull trend, even one sideways bar. Ours needs a pole first, a fast run, and then a short, tight rest. So when you read his material, a lot of his flags are pauses we'd never call a flag. When we say flag, find the pole first.
questions.lesson_line: Same words, different pattern. Ours starts with a pole.
questions.simple: False. Brooks uses the name for any small pullback, but ours rests after a fast run, so it needs a pole.

deeper.trap: The same words can name two ideas. Brooks counts a one-bar pause as a bull flag. A search for the name in his material will list pauses that we would not call a flag.

the card's pole line is the other half

questions.q: By our card, take it or pass?
choices: Pass; the lines are not stacked up
Take it; price is above the 200-day
Take it; the pole is strong
Pass; the flag is only five days
questions.answer: Pass; the lines are not stacked up
questions.why: Pass. Our card wants the 50-day above the 200-day and rising, with the close above the 50-day. Here the 50-day is still under the 200-day. Our rulebook only bars longs below the 200-day, so this extra test is the card's own.
questions.lesson_line: Check the lines before the flag. Stacked and rising, or pass.

wrong.Take it; price is above the 200-day: Price above the 200 is one line. By our card the 50 under the 200 fails the other.
wrong.Take it; the pole is strong: The pole is the pattern. The averages are the context, and they are out of order.
wrong.Pass; the flag is only five days: Five days is a normal short rest for a flag. The fault is in the averages, not the length.

questions.story: A 40% pole and a tidy five-day flag. Price is above the 200-day, but the 50-day still sits under the 200-day after a long decline.
questions.simple: The 50-day average is still under the 200-day, so by our card the stock has not fully recovered and we pass.

deeper.counter: The rulebook line is looser than the card. Price above the 200-day passes the rulebook's long test. The card adds that the 50-day must be above the 200-day and rising. A stock repairing a long decline can pass the first test and fail the second.

The stop was set too close
The pole was too small to trust
The flag was too deep to buy

wrong.The flag was too deep to buy: It was only 3.8% deep after a 30% pole. Depth wasn't the problem.

questions.q: A flag in a stock that trades 2 million shares a day. Your stop and risk allow 60,000 shares. How many do you buy?
choices: No more than 20,000 shares
No more than 10,000 shares
No more than 40,000 shares
No more than 60,000 shares
questions.answer: No more than 20,000 shares
questions.why: 20,000 at most. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 2 million is 20,000. Own more than that and your own selling moves the price against you when you need out. Your stop says 60,000. The volume says 20,000. You take the smaller. Splitting the buy into pieces doesn't help, because the cap is on what you own.
questions.lesson_line: Size is the smaller of what the stop allows and what the volume can carry.

wrong.No more than 10,000 shares: That's half the cap. One percent of 2 million is 20,000.
wrong.No more than 40,000 shares: That's twice the volume cap. We never own more than 1% of daily volume.
wrong.No more than 60,000 shares: That's what the stop allows. The volume cap is smaller, and the smaller one wins.

questions.simple: 20,000 at most. We own no more than 1% of daily volume, so we can still get out.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a split buy slips under the cap. Three pieces still leave you owning all of it. The cap is on what you own, not on any one order. Work out the volume cap first, then check the stop size against it.

reasons: a computed key

questions.q: Write tomorrow's plan. Entry, stop, first sell?

Limit under, mental stop, sell a push
Market buy, mental stop, no sell plan
Buy the close, day-low stop, no sell

questions.q: What do you do with the position?
choices: Sell a big part into the strength
Add, the trend is speeding up
Hold it all for the measured move
Nothing, let the trail handle it
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the strength
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. Three gap-ups in a row on rising volume, way above the 9 EMA, is a climax. That's the last fast leg of a run, where it's most stretched and buyers are most eager. Those are the buyers you sell to. How big a part is my judgment, and it depends on how wild it gets. Keep a piece on the trail in case it keeps going. Just don't give the whole move back waiting.
questions.lesson_line: When the whole move happens in three days, that's the strength to sell into.

wrong.Hold it all for the measured move: A measured move is a guess. A climax is right in front of you, so sell a big part into it.
wrong.Add, the trend is speeding up: Not into a climax. That's where you sell, not buy. Adding to a winner is rare and a feel call.
wrong.Nothing, let the trail handle it: The trail is for the part you keep. By the time a climax closes under the 9 EMA, a lot is given back.

questions.story: Three weeks after your flag buy, the stock gaps up three mornings in a row on rising volume. It closes far above its 9 EMA.
questions.simple: Three gap-ups like that are a climax, so sell a big part while buyers are still eager.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading three gap-ups as proof the trend will go on. A climax is a burst of gaps and expanding bars far above the 9 EMA. You sell a big part into it, and how big is a judgment call, not a number.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34), which is a judgment call
fixed before: story split

questions.q: You got stopped out of a flag yesterday. You still like the stock. You buy it again only if it triggers again, as a new trade.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Getting stopped out means this try didn't work. Liking the stock isn't a reason to get back in. A new trigger is. When it comes, it's a brand new trade: fresh entry, fresh stop under that day's low, size worked out again. Jumping back in just because you want it back is how one small loss turns into a pile of them.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped out means flat. The next trade needs its own trigger.
questions.simple: True. After a stop-out you're flat, and only a fresh trigger puts you back in, never just wanting it.

deeper.trap: Wanting back in is the pull. Liking the stock isn't a trigger. Ask one question: has the setup triggered again? If yes, it's a new trade with a new stop, sized fresh. If no, you stay flat.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21)

questions.q: What does that strong close tell you about the trade?
choices: Not much, strong closes fail too
It's a lock, these rarely fail
Move the stop to breakeven now
Sell it, the volume was too low
questions.answer: Not much, strong closes fail too
questions.why: Not much on its own. QCOM is this chart. It closed the trigger day right at the high on 0.76x volume, and that day was the top. The next session took the stop. Three of our four failed flags closed the trigger day at the high and still failed. Light volume on the break is a mark against it, but it's not an exit. The stop is the exit, so leave it where it is.
questions.lesson_line: A strong close is a good sign, not a promise. The stop stays put.

wrong.It's a lock, these rarely fail: QCOM, STZ and LLY all closed the trigger day at the high and were stopped within days.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven now: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. Not after one good close.
wrong.Sell it, the volume was too low: Light volume is a mark against it, not an exit. The stop is the exit.

questions.story: You bought the flag break. The day closes right at its high, but on below-average volume.
questions.simple: Not much. A strong close isn't a promise, and three of our four failed flags closed at the high too.

deeper.example: Two of the failures show it. QCOM closed the trigger day at the high on 0.76x volume and was the top. STZ closed at the high on 0.32x volume and was stopped on day 2. Bonde wants a close near the high on a higher-volume breakout day. A strong close alone made the day look good, but the stop decided the trade.

reasons: the breakout volume line is still pending (D-006)
the count of failures is our own scan

questions.q: What is the better plan?
choices: Wait for the tight day; stop under it
Buy today; use the flag low as the stop
Buy today at half the usual size
Buy today with a 3% stop instead
questions.answer: Wait for the tight day; stop under it
questions.why: Wait for the tight day. An inside day or narrow-range day right before the trigger is the A+ tightness cue, because it gives a nearer stop. Bonde wants the day before a breakout to be a narrow-range or down day. The stop comes first and the size comes from it. A 4.6% stop today can fit inside 3% tomorrow if the day stays tight.
questions.lesson_line: A tighter day is a tighter stop. One more day of patience buys the size.

wrong.Buy today; use the flag low as the stop: The flag low is the invalidation, not the stop. It is almost never a 3% stop.
wrong.Buy today at half the usual size: Fewer shares is allowed, but the stop is still 4.6% wide. The tight day can bring it inside 3%.
wrong.Buy today with a 3% stop instead: The stop is a few cents under the day's low, set first. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Do not squeeze the stop.

questions.story: The flag's wide day four leaves the honest stop 4.6% under the break. The stock looks ready to print a narrow inside day tomorrow.
questions.simple: A narrow day right before the trigger gives you a nearer stop, so waiting a day is the better plan.

deeper.trap: Size follows the stop, never the reverse. Cutting shares to fit a wide stop is allowed, but it does not make the stop nearer. Forcing the stop to 3% when the honest stop is 4.6% puts the stop where the setup does not.

reasons: rests on the owner's stop-first rule (A3) and the 3% habit (A13)
fixed before: the half-size note

questions.q: Do you take it or pass?
choices: Take it, every close held the line
Pass, two closes sat under it
Pass, the pole was too small
Take it, the rest ran four days
questions.answer: Take it, every close held the line
questions.why: Take it. Every close in this eight-day flag held the rising 20 EMA. Buyers defended the line every single day. That's a picture perfect flag. SHOP is the chart: a 99% pole in 12 days to 66.57, then eight sessions between 59.50 and 66.26. It triggered at 62.80 with a stop at 61.65, just 1.8% away, and went on to 41.7R.
questions.lesson_line: The flag that never closes under its line is the one worth the alert.

wrong.Pass, two closes sat under it: Look again. Every close sits on or above the 20 EMA.
wrong.Pass, the pole was too small: The pole nearly doubled in 12 days. Small isn't the word.
wrong.Take it, the rest ran four days: Right call, wrong reason. The rest ran eight sessions. Count the bars before you give a reason.

questions.simple: Every close held the rising 20 EMA, so buyers defended it every day, and the flag is intact.

deeper.trap: An intraday dip under the line that closes back above is fine, and it's often the buy. What ends a flag is a close under the line that isn't taken back the next day.

reasons: a chart question read off our own bars
the 41.7R run is from our own scan

questions.story: The day before the buy. Read this flag against its rising 20 EMA, close by close.

questions.q: Do you take it or pass?
choices: Pass, the highs rose, a wedge up
Take it, the pole was 58%
Take it, it's only 10.7% deep
Pass, the flag ran too long
questions.answer: Pass, the highs rose, a wedge up
questions.why: Pass. The highs climbed 5.6% across this seven-day pause. A pause that keeps climbing never rested. That's a wedge up, not a flag, and I don't buy it. BA had everything else going for it: a 58% pole and a pause only 10.7% deep. That's what makes it a good trap. Check the slope of the highs, not just the depth.
questions.lesson_line: A rest that climbs isn't resting. Flat or down is the flag. Up is a pass.

wrong.Take it, the pole was 58%: The pole was fine. The pause after it climbed, and a climbing pause is a wedge up.
wrong.Take it, it's only 10.7% deep: Depth isn't the problem here. The slope of the highs is.
wrong.Pass, the flag ran too long: Right call, wrong reason. Seven sessions is a normal rest. It's the climbing highs.

questions.simple: Pass. The highs kept climbing through the pause, so it never rested, and a rising pause is a wedge up.

deeper.counter: Zanger: a bull flag has lower tops and lower bottoms with parallel lines. Bulkowski finds the best flags tilt down after an upward trend.

reasons: the wedge-up line is the card's proposal
a chart question read off our own bars

questions.story: The day before it trades over the prior day's high. Look at the slope of the highs through the pause.

questions.q: Which run makes the better flag pole?
questions.story: VQRT jumped 45% in five sessions on an earnings gap. LZNB drifted up 35% over fifteen sessions on no news. Both are now pausing.
choices: VQRT, fast, on a catalyst
LZNB, a longer, steady climb
Both make the same pole
Neither, a pole can't have news
questions.answer: VQRT, fast, on a catalyst
questions.why: VQRT. A flag rests after a sharp, fast run, and 45% in five sessions on an earnings gap is exactly that. There's a real reason behind the move, so buyers have a reason to come back. LZNB's 35% over fifteen sessions on no news is a slow climb, and the pause after it has less to rest from. Earnings gaps make great poles. Five of our ten flag examples had the report inside the pole.
questions.lesson_line: A flag rests after a sharp, fast run with a reason behind it.

wrong.Both make the same pole: They don't. The fast run on a real catalyst is the one a flag rests from best.
wrong.LZNB, a longer, steady climb: A steady climb on no news is a trend, not a burst. The pause after it has less to rest from.
wrong.Neither, a pole can't have news: News isn't a flaw. A sharp run on a real catalyst, like an earnings gap, is what we want.

questions.simple: VQRT, because a flag rests after a sharp, fast run, and a gap on earnings is just that.

reasons: rests on the card's grade row for the A+ pole

deeper.counter: Bulkowski wants a flagpole that is unusually steep and lasts several days, and his earnings flag starts with a near vertical run.

questions.q: Before the pole, the lowest low was 40.00. What price is 30% above it?
questions.why: 52.00. Add 30% to the low of 40.00. On our card, a pole of 30% or more, made fast on a catalyst, is the A+ pole.
questions.lesson_line: Know the 30% line before you call a pole A+.
questions.simple: Add 30% to the low to find the price where the pole reaches the A+ line.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the card's grade row

wrong.$57.14: Divided by the remainder instead of adding the gain.

questions.q: Which flag has the A+ depth on our card?
questions.story: Two flags follow strong poles. Flag A gave back 20% of its pole and sits 12% under the top. Flag B gave back 30% and sits 9% under the top.
choices: Flag B; it passes both of the tests
Flag A; it gave back less of its pole
Both; each passes one of the tests
Neither; both gave back too much
questions.answer: Flag B; it passes both of the tests
questions.why: Flag B. Our card's A+ depth cue needs both: a third of the pole or less, and 10% or less from the top. Flag B gave back 30% and sits 9% under the top, so it clears both. Flag A gave back 20%, which is fine, but sits 12% under the top, so it fails one.
questions.lesson_line: Our card's A+ depth: a third of the pole or less, within 10% of the top.

wrong.Flag A; it gave back less of its pole: Flag A passes the pole test but sits 12% under the top. The card needs both.
wrong.Both; each passes one of the tests: Flag B passes both tests. Flag A fails the 10% test.
wrong.Neither; both gave back too much: Flag B gave back 30%, under a third of the pole, and sits 9% under the top. It passes both.

questions.simple: Flag B has the A+ depth, because it passes both the one-third and the 10% tests.

deeper.example: Flag B gave back 30%, under a third of the pole, and sits 9% under the top, inside 10%. Both hold. Flag A gave back 20%, under a third, but sits 12% under the top, over 10%. Only one holds. The card asks for both, so Flag A is not the A+ depth.

reasons: one cited fact only (c45)
the card's depth cue is a proposal, not a settled rule
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: The pole top is 60.00 and the flag low is 56.00. How far under the top is the low, as a percent of the top?
questions.why: 6.7%. Take the top minus the low, 60.00 minus 56.00, and divide by the top, not by the low. On our card, 10% or less from the top is one part of the A+ depth cue, and 6.7% fits it. The other part is a third of the pole or less.
questions.lesson_line: Measure depth from the top, in percent.
questions.simple: The low is 6.7 percent under the top, found by dividing the drop by the 60.00 top.

reasons: one cited fact only (c45)
the card's depth cue is a proposal, not a settled rule
a computed key
fixed before by the checker

wrong.7.1%: Divided the drop by the low instead of the top.
wrong.93.3%: Took the low as a percent of the top and skipped the drop.
wrong.107.1%: Took the top as a percent of the low, skipping the subtraction.

questions.q: You'd buy the trigger at 56.60. The 9 EMA is at 50.00. How far above the 9 EMA is that buy?
questions.why: 13.2%. Take 56.60 minus 50.00, then divide by the EMA, 50.00, not by your buy price. That's past our 10% line, so I skip it. The further a stock stands above its 9 EMA, the more a normal pullback to the line costs you. Wait for the line to catch up, or for a tighter spot closer to it.
questions.lesson_line: Check the stretch before you buy. More than 10% over the 9 EMA, skip.
questions.simple: The buy is 13.2 percent above the 9 EMA, past our 10 percent line, so we skip it.
