rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)
a computed key

wrong.11.7%: You divided by your buy price. Divide by the average, 50.00.
wrong.6.6%: That's the dollar gap, 6.60, read as a percent.
wrong.1.3%: A decimal slip. Move the point one place right.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Skip a long that is more than ___% above its 9 EMA.
questions.why: 10. Too stretched to buy: we skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA. The 4% in the no-chase rule is a different limit, measured from the buy point, not from the 9 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Over 10% above the 9 EMA is too stretched. Wait for the line to catch up.
questions.simple: The blank is 10, because we skip a long that is more than 10 percent above its 9 EMA.

reasons: one cited fact only (h13)
rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)

questions.q: Where does your stop go now?
questions.story: You bought the flag break at 20.09 with the stop at 19.81. It pushes up for several days, and you sell your first piece into the push.
choices: Up to your entry, 20.09
Down, to give it more room
Cancel it, a piece is banked
Switch to the 9 EMA trail now
questions.answer: Up to your entry, 20.09
questions.why: Up to your entry, 20.09. Moving the stop to breakeven means a trade that's working can't turn into a loss. You can do it anywhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell like here. Some of the gain is banked, and the rest is now a free ride. The stop only ever moves up, and it stays a real order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: At the first sell, the stop can come up to your entry.

wrong.Switch to the 9 EMA trail now: The trail is for later, once it's run. Right now the stop comes up to your entry.
wrong.Down, to give it more room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Cancel it, a piece is banked: Every position keeps a real stop with the broker. Selling a piece doesn't change that.

questions.simple: Up to your entry, so a trade that's working can't turn into a loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook breakeven rule (B19)
the 2R to 5R window is a range

questions.q: Your flag trade is up 3R and you haven't sold anything yet. Moving your stop up to breakeven now is allowed.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. 3R sits inside the window. We can move the stop to breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell. It's a judgment, not a fixed number, so where in that window is your call. Once it's at breakeven, a winning trade can't turn into a loser. Either way, the stop only ever moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven is a judgment: anywhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell.
questions.simple: True. Anywhere from 2R to 5R is fine, and at breakeven a winner can't turn into a loser.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook breakeven rule (B19)

questions.q: Is the flag still a buy?
questions.story: A tight flag rests on the 20 EMA. On two of its days the stock closed red on 1.6 times its 50-day average volume. Today is quiet. A setup's grade is our judgment of how clean it is, and it sets the size.
choices: Yes; two heavy days lower the grade
No; that is distribution, not a rest
Yes; heavy red days are normal in flags
No; any red close ends a flag
questions.answer: Yes; two heavy days lower the grade
questions.why: Yes, at a lower grade. Two red closes on 1.6 times the 50-day average volume are heavy selling, a warning to be mindful of. They lower the grade, our judgment of how clean the setup is, and a lower grade means a smaller size. They do not end the flag, and it still holds the 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Two heavy red days are a warning and a lower grade, not the end of the flag.

wrong.Yes; heavy red days are normal in flags: Heavy red days are not normal. They are selling to be mindful of, and they lower the grade.
wrong.No; any red close ends a flag: A plain red close does not end a flag. Even a heavy red day only lowers the grade.
wrong.No; that is distribution, not a rest: Heavy red days are a distribution warning. They lower the grade, but they do not void the flag.

questions.simple: Yes, but smaller. Two heavy red days warn of selling and lower the grade, but the flag still holds its 20 EMA.

deeper.trap: Do not read heavy red days as a veto, and do not ignore them either. Each one is a warning and lowers the grade. The flag still ends on a close under the 20 EMA that is not reclaimed, not on volume.

reasons: rests on the settled HEAVY-DOWN ruling (2026-11-14)
the 1.5x line is a card number

questions.q: The 50-day average volume is 1,800,000 shares. A red flag day trades 2,700,000. How many times average is that?
questions.answer: 1.5 times
questions.why: 1.5 times. Divide the day's volume of 2,700,000 by the average of 1,800,000. That is right on the line: on our card, a red day on 1.5 times average volume or more is heavy. A heavy red day is a warning that lowers the grade.
questions.lesson_line: Divide the day's volume by the average. 1.5 times or more is heavy, a warning.
questions.simple: Divide the day's volume by the average to get 1.5 times, which is right at the heavy line.

reasons: a computed key
the 1.5x line is a card number

choices: 0.5 times
0.7 times
1.5 times
15 times

wrong.0.5 times: Counted only the extra volume above average.
wrong.0.7 times: Flipped the division: average over the day's volume.
wrong.15 times: Decimal slip: moved the decimal one place.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought a flag break two days ago. It's down about half an R, and your stop hasn't traded. A post on your feed says the market looks weak.
choices: Hold it, the stop is the plan
Sell half now to be safe
Widen the stop to give it room
Move the stop up to your entry
questions.answer: Hold it, the stop is the plan
questions.why: Hold it. Your stop is your exit, set where the idea fails. It hasn't traded, so the idea is still alive. Down half an R two days in is normal noise. A post on your feed is someone else's opinion, not your plan. The only other exit is the time stop: still under 1R after 10 trading days, you sell. Until one of those hits, let it work.
questions.lesson_line: After the entry, the stop is the exit. Not a post, not a hunch.

wrong.Sell half now to be safe: A post isn't an exit. The stop is, along with the time stop.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Move the stop up to your entry: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. You're below your entry, so it would hit right away.

questions.simple: Hold. The stop marks where the idea fails, it hasn't traded, and a post is no reason to sell.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, C33)

questions.q: The market filter in the app reads Orange. You have an A+ flag and two B flags triggering. You take only the A+.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Orange means the market's under pressure, one step from Red. Breakouts fail more often when the market isn't backing them. So I only want my very best idea, the cleanest flag with the tightest risk. A+ is the grade we give our cleanest setups. The two B flags can wait for a better market. Green is when we press. Red is mostly cash.
questions.lesson_line: Orange keeps only the A+ flags. Red is mostly cash.
questions.simple: True. Orange is a weak market, so we take only our cleanest setups, the A+ ones.

reasons: rests on the owner's market reading (F65)

questions.q: A tight bull flag forms, but the stock is below its 200-day moving average. Do you buy it?
choices: No, not under the 200-day
Yes, at half size to be safe
Yes, if volume dries up
Yes, with a tighter stop
questions.answer: No, not under the 200-day
questions.why: No. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line. The 200-day separates a long-term uptrend from a downtrend. Under it, a flag is just a pause inside a stock that's falling. A smaller size or a tighter stop changes how much you lose, not which way the stock is going. Wait until it's back above the line, or find a leader that never left it.
questions.lesson_line: Below the 200-day there's no flag to buy.

wrong.Yes, at half size to be safe: Half size doesn't fix it. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, at any size.
wrong.Yes, if volume dries up: Volume that dries up raises the grade. It doesn't lift the 200-day line.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop: A tighter stop changes the size, not the trend. Under the 200-day, we pass.

questions.simple: No. Under the 200-day a stock is in a downtrend, so a flag there is just a pause in a fall.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

deeper.counter: The only exception we make is for indexes and leveraged ETFs, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. Never for a single stock.

questions.q: Great-looking flag. It sits just under its trigger level, and that level hasn't traded yet. Do you buy now or wait?
choices: Wait, no sign buyers are back yet
Buy now, you get a better price
Buy now, the 9 EMA crossed the 20
Wait for volume to peak in the flag
questions.answer: Wait, no sign buyers are back yet
questions.why: Wait. Until the level trades, nothing shows buyers are back. The rest can still roll over into a bigger drop, and you'd own it with no clear line to risk against. The trigger is the first proof. When it trades, buy at market, with the stop a few cents under the low of the day. Buying early inside the flag is guessing, and guessing costs more than the few cents you save.

wrong.Buy now, you get a better price: A few cents better isn't worth owning it before there's any proof. Pay up a little for the trigger.
wrong.Buy now, the 9 EMA crossed the 20: A crossing isn't our entry. The trigger level trading is.
wrong.Wait for volume to peak in the flag: Volume dries up while a flag rests. The loud day is the break itself, so there's no peak to wait for.

questions.simple: Wait. Until the level trades, the rest may not be over, and the trigger is the first sign buyers are back.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for the trigger. It's the first proof that buyers are back.

reasons: Bulkowski and ChartSchool agree: buy on the break, not before; our rule D-003 says the trigger is always the entry

deeper.counter: Bulkowski says to buy when price pierces the flag's trendline or rises above the pattern's high, but not before. ChartSchool adds that more volume on the break lends credence.
